Your job is to make the real renderer produce frames that hold up next to them, from real storyboard data of any length, and to add what a still cannot show: the lens gliding from scene to scene and the pencil marks drawing on.

This is the part of the product people will actually see. Spend your effort on how the frames look and move. Look at your own rendered stills often, and be honest about which ones are weaker than the reference.

There is no `.env` and there are no API keys in this checkout, by design. Rendering needs the network for fonts and a browser download; that is expected.

Commit after each green test cycle. Finish by running the reel package's tests and `pnpm typecheck` at the repo root.

End with a short report: what exists now, test counts, which frames you consider weakest and why, and every deviation from the plan with the reason.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/yehor/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/frontend-design/f359d43b4060/skills/frontend-design

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.

## Ground your designs in the subject matter

If the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.

Choose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Default to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.

Avoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:
- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.
- Using all caps for labels.
- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.

Visual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.

Use non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique

For calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:
1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);
2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;
3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;
4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;
5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.

All traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.
- Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- Type: the typefaces and their roles.
- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?
- Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the tone conversational: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each written element do exactly one job.

1	# Dailies Core Implementation Plan
2	
3	> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.
4	
5	**Goal:** From a repository URL, produce a fact-checked, narrated MP4 reel of its recorded coding-agent sessions through a resumable pipeline and a CLI.
6	
7	**Architecture:** A pnpm TypeScript monorepo. `packages/core` holds every shared schema; each other package exposes plain functions over those schemas. A durable runner executes stages in order and persists each stage's artifact so a run can resume.
8	
9	**Tech Stack:** Node 22+, pnpm workspaces, TypeScript (strict, ESM), zod, vitest, OpenAI SDK against an OpenAI-compatible gateway, neatlogs SDK, Remotion 4, better-sqlite3, ffmpeg, git, Entire CLI.
10	
11	**Spec:** `docs/specs/2026-10-11-dailies-design.md`
12	
13	This plan covers Tier 1 of the spec. The web app, evaluation harness, runtime read-back and deployment are separate plans that build on the interfaces fixed here.
14	
15	## Global Constraints
16	
17	- Node `>=22`. TypeScript `strict: true`, `"type": "module"`, `moduleResolution: "bundler"`.
18	- Internal packages are consumed as TypeScript source: `"exports": { ".": "./src/index.ts" }`. No build step; run with `tsx`, check with `tsc --noEmit`.
19	- Package names: `@dailies/core`, `@dailies/ingest`, `@dailies/agent`, `@dailies/verify`, `@dailies/voice`, `@dailies/reel`, `@dailies/pipeline`, `@dailies/cli`.
20	- A package imports another only through its index. Shared types live in `@dailies/core` and nowhere else.
21	- A task edits files only inside the directories listed under its **Files**. Do not change another package's `package.json`.
22	- Tests: vitest, files `packages/<name>/test/*.test.ts`. Run one package with `pnpm --filter @dailies/<name> test`.
23	- No secret ever enters the repository. Configuration comes from `.env` through `loadEnv()`.
24	- Every model call goes through `@dailies/agent`. No other package imports `openai`.
25	- Model ids on the gateway: `claude-sonnet-4.6`, `claude-haiku`, `nova-pro`. Gateway base URL: `LITELLM_BASE_URL`. Stay under 50 requests per minute.
26	- Trace endpoint: `https://ingest.neatlogs.com`.
27	- A verdict is `verified` only on positive evidence. Anything unknown is `unverifiable`, never `verified` and never `contradicted`.
28	- Commit after every green test cycle with a short imperative message.
29	- Once code exists, locate it with `entire graph search` before broad grep, as `CLAUDE.md` instructs.
30	
31	## Review Focus
32	
33	1. A repository with no checkpoints, or none inside the window: the run ends early with a clear message and no render. Pinned in Task 2 and Task 10.
34	2. A tool result of several megabytes or with ANSI colour codes: entries are truncated head-and-tail, colour codes are stripped, memory stays flat. Pinned in Task 2 and Task 4.
35	3. A claim quote that differs from the transcript only by whitespace or Markdown marks: still matched. A quote that is not in the entry: dropped. Pinned in Task 4.
36	4. A test run whose output the parser does not recognise: `unknown`, so the claim is `unverifiable`. Pinned in Task 4.
37	5. Narration audio whose pause count does not equal the line count: timings fall back to proportional alignment and never throw. Pinned in Task 5.
38	6. A model reply that is not valid JSON for the schema: one repair turn, then the stage fails and the runner retries it. Pinned in Task 3.
39	7. A secret inside a human prompt or a tool result: redacted at ingest, before any model or renderer sees it. Pinned in Task 1 and Task 2.

Extract the claims the coding agent made, then judge each one.

Extraction: a small model reads assistant messages at turn ends and returns claims with the exact quote and the entry id. A claim is kept only if its quote is found in that entry (compared after collapsing whitespace and Markdown marks).

| Claim kind | Evidence | Verdict rule |
|---|---|---|
| `tests_pass` | last test-runner call in the session before the claim, and its output | verified if it passed; contradicted if it failed; stale if code was edited after the last passing run; unverifiable if no run exists |
| `build_passes` | same for build, type-check and lint commands | same |
| `ran_command` | a matching tool call and its result | verified if it succeeded; contradicted if it errored; unverifiable if no matching call is recorded |
| `fixed_error` | the error text in an earlier tool result and a later run of the same command without it | unverifiable when no later run exists |
| `implemented` | the diff of the linked commits | a second model must quote the supporting hunk; the quote is validated against the diff |

The first four are decided by deterministic parsers over the recorded tool results. Only `implemented` uses a model, from a different model family than the writer, and its quoted evidence is checked mechanically.

**4.4 Script**
The writer produces a storyboard: ordered scenes with typed props and narration lines. The reel follows one arc: the problem (the human's request), the key decisions, the implementation, and the recorded validation. Each line carries evidence refs. Contradicted and stale claims become flag scenes. Unverifiable claims are either left out or stated as unverified.

**4.5 Ground (gate, in code)**
For every line: evidence refs must resolve; every number in the sentence must appear in the facts computed for that scene; a second model must find the sentence entailed by the evidence. A failing line is rewritten up to twice, then dropped. A style lint (banned phrases, sentence length) runs here too. The on-screen text and narration are scanned again for secrets. The stage reports how many lines were dropped.

**4.6 Voice**
Gemini text-to-speech per line, cached by content hash. Measured durations drive the timeline. On failure: retry with backoff, then an alternate voice, then a captions-only cut that is labelled as such.

**4.7 Footage**
Scenes are rendered from data: title, quoted prompt, terminal replay, animated diff, stats, claim-versus-record flag, end card. Tier 3 adds a session timeline, the dependency-graph scene and a Playwright recording of the live app when the repo declares a URL.

**4.8 Render**
Remotion composes the storyboard into 1080p30 MP4, an SRT file and a poster frame.

**4.9 Review (agent)**
Deterministic checks first: total duration against target, silent gaps, black frames, per-scene text limits. Then frames from each scene go to a vision model with a fixed rubric (legibility, overflow, wrong or empty content). Findings map to fixes (shorten a line, change scene parameters, regenerate audio) and the run loops back, at most twice.

**4.10 Gate (in code)**
All must hold: grounding passed, secret scan clean, review passed, cost within budget, human approval recorded. Failure of any condition blocks publishing; there is no override path in the worker.

**4.11 Publish**

# Dailies design reference: Loupe

The night's work is a strip of film lying on a switched-off lightbox. A loupe moves along it.
What sits under the glass is what the narrator is talking about, and the only lit thing in the
room is the frame that matters.

The anchor is a photo editor's 4× illuminated loupe on 35 mm stock, and the contact-sheet habit
of marking selects in grease pencil. Everything below follows from those two objects.

The reel renderer (`packages/reel`) is the first implementation. Its tokens live in
`packages/reel/src/theme.ts`; nothing under `src/remotion` carries a colour, a size or a family
of its own.

## Colour

| Token | Value | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `lightbox.far` | `#0d1211` | the room, far from the lens |
| `lightbox.glass` | `#121917` | the lightbox surface |
| `lightbox.near` | `#1a2421` | light spilling around the lens |
| `film.base` | `#070a09` | unexposed film between and around frames |
| `film.frame` | `#131c19` | a frame's picture area, unlit |
| `film.perf` | `#1c2724` | the lightbox seen through a perforation |
| `film.lit` | `#2a3f38` | the picture area under the glass |
| `white` | `#eef3f1` | type and lit detail |
| `soft` | `#c3cfca` | secondary type |
| `muted` | `#8fa099` | tertiary type |
| `pencil` | `#ffd60a` | grease pencil, and the verdict pill |
| `ink` | `#0d1211` | type on pencil yellow |

The surface runs from `#0d1211` to `#1a2421`. Yellow is the only accent and it means a verdict.
Added and removed lines in a patch are told apart by weight and brightness, not by hue.

The far field is darker than the black threshold of `ffmpeg blackdetect`, which the review stage
runs. A frame still never reads as black, because the lit glass is in every frame and covers far
more than the two percent of pixels that check needs. `theme.test.ts` pins the luma of `film.lit`
and the smallest share of the frame the glass may cover.

## Type

| Role | Family | Weights | Floor at 1920×1080 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Display | Unbounded | 300, 600, 800 | 72 px |
| Text | Figtree (Manrope for Cyrillic and Greek, which Figtree lacks) | 500, 600 | 40 px |
| Code | Martian Mono at 75 % width | 400, 500 | 30 px |

Display is for the thing a frame is about: a repo name, a figure, a short quote. Text is for
labels, long quotes and captions. Code is for commands, patches and source references.

Sizes are fitted to measured glyph widths, between the largest size the composition allows and
the floor of the role. Nothing is set below its floor. A string that cannot fit its frame at the
display floor is set in the text face instead of being cut; only when that fails too is it
shortened with an ellipsis.

Two things are texture and not text, and are exempt from the floors: the film's edge print
(`DAILIES SAFETY FILM`, frame numbers) and the lettering engraved on the loupe's rim. They are
there to be recognised, not read.

## Space, radius, stroke

Spacing scale, in px: 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 72, 112.

Radii: pills and the loupe are fully round; the caption bar is 20 px; a frame's picture area and
the perforations are rounded in proportion to the film (about 1 % of the frame pitch).

The whole strip is tilted two degrees anticlockwise, and so is everything seen through the glass.

## The film strip

A horizontal strip of 35 mm stock: a dark base, a row of rounded perforations along each edge, a
hairline of light on both edges, and picture frames. A full frame is eight perforations long and
landscape; a half-frame is four perforations long and portrait. Each scene's content lives on
frames of the strip.

The strip is one continuous object for the whole reel. A scene frames a stretch of it at its own
magnification, so moving to the next scene is a camera move along the film, not a cut: the strip
advances and scales, the perforations stay in phase. While a scene plays the picture drifts
slowly along the strip.

Frames that carry nothing for the current scene hold greeked content: a few soft bars.

## The loupe

One lens, drawn by one component (`Loupe.tsx`): a clear skirt that refracts the film beneath it,
a knurled barrel, a rim engraved `DAILIES OPTICAL 4× ILLUMINATED LOUPE`, glass with a soft
highlight, and a shadow on the lightbox.

The loupe is a persistent layer of the composition and belongs to no scene. Each scene declares
where the lens rests, how large it is and how the barrel is turned (`lens.ts`). Between scenes
the lens glides from one resting place to the next on a spring; the move starts a little before
the cut and lands after it. What is under the glass is shown enlarged, and it slides through the
glass faster than the lens travels, the way a real loupe passes over print. It comes into focus
as the lens lands.

Text never touches the rim: content is fitted to the chord of the glass at the height of each
line, less a margin.

## Pencil grammar

Four marks, drawn in yellow grease pencil with a wobbling, waxy stroke. They are used everywhere
and nothing else carries these meanings.

| Mark | Meaning |
|---|---|
| a closed ring | verified |
| a cross | contradicted |
| a dashed ring | stale |
| a question mark | unverified |

A mark draws on, as a stroke, while the line it belongs to is spoken. Marks pass behind type,
which keeps a halo of the frame's colour, so a crossed-out quote stays readable.

The verdict of a flagged claim is also set in words on a yellow pill.

## Scenes

**Title.** The lens rests on the repo name, set in display inside the glass. The window label is
set large beside it, with the session and commit counts under it and the wordmark in the corner.
The strip passes behind with greeked frames.

**Prompt.** The lens grows until the glass fills the frame. Through it: `You asked`, the human's
request, and its session reference in code. A short request is set in display; a long one in the
text face.

**Terminal.** One frame per step. A frame carries the command, the decisive part of its output
set large (`2 failed`, `14 passed`), the rest of the result under it, and its source reference.
The lens holds still while the strip advances a frame at a time, so the step being spoken is the
one under the glass and the steps already told sit to its left. A passing step is ringed; a
failing step is crossed. The scene comes to rest on the last step.

**Diff.** The largest lens. Through it: the file name in display with its directory in code, the
added and removed counts, and the patch in code. Added lines sit on a faint band of light at
full strength; removed lines are dimmed. When the patch is longer than the glass, the window
with the most changed lines is shown and the rest is counted.

**Stats.** One half-frame per value, the figure in display over its label. The lens rests on the
first value and shows it enlarged; the others follow to its right. Figures count up as the lens
lands.

**Flag.** On the left, a frame with the agent's quote under `the agent said` and the pencil
through it: a cross for a contradicted claim, a dashed ring around a stale one. Beside it the
lens rests on the recorded reality, which is ringed. The verdict sits between them on a yellow
pill, `CONTRADICTED` or `STALE`, and the source reference is printed on the film's edge under
the quote.

**End.** The repo name; a strip of small frames with one mark per claim, rings for verified,
crosses for flagged, question marks for unverified, in that order, at most 16 with `+n` after
them; under it the three counts in words. The lens rests at the end of the strip over the
wordmark.

## Captions

A captions-only cut shows the line being spoken in a bar at the bottom of the frame: film-base
black, 20 px radius, text face, up to three lines. Every narrated scene moves up to keep that
inset clear. A voiced cut has no bar and uses the full frame.

## Motion

- The lens glide and the film advance between scenes share one spring.
- The strip advances a frame at a time inside the terminal scene.
- Pencil marks draw on with their line; the verdict pill stamps down after its mark.
- Figures count up; content under the glass pulls into focus.
- Everything except the marks has landed before the middle of its scene.

Review stills are taken at the middle of each scene, as the captions cut, with every mark and
every step already landed, so a still shows all a scene will hold.
